PROJECT HIGHLIGHT

This project evaluated whether biofilters (a common type of stormwater treatment system) can capture microplastic pollution washing off urban streets and parking lots. Researchers monitored seven biofilters across southern California during 18 rainstorms and found they removed a median of 72% of microplastics from runoff, achieving nearly complete removal during some storms. The study identified specific design features that make these biofilters more effective at trapping microplastics before they reach the ocean.

 

PROJECT SUMMARY

When rain falls on cities, it washes pollution off streets, parking lots and roofs into storm drains that typically flow directly to streams and the ocean. To clean this polluted runoff, many communities install biofilters: treatment systems that filter water through layers of material such as sand and compost layers before being discharged. While these biofilters were designed to remove common pollutants, few studies have analyzed whether they also remove microplastics, the tiny plastic fragments that are increasingly recognized as a threat to marine life.

Researchers partnered with stormwater management agencies across Southern California to study seven biofilters during rainstorms. They collected water samples entering and leaving each biofilter, as well as samples of the filter material itself. The results showed these biofilters are highly effective: they reduced microplastic levels by a median of 72%, with the best performance removing over 99% during a single storm. By examining the filter materials under microscopes, researchers discovered that the tiny spaces between particles act like nets, trapping plastic fragments as water flows through. Biofilters with more small spaces (less than 20 millionths of a meter) captured more microplastics, providing a practical guideline for designing better systems in the future.

Beyond the research findings, the project trained five undergraduate students in advanced microplastic analysis techniques and hosted workshops for 41 engineering students from three California universities. These educational efforts help build the workforce needed to design and maintain stormwater management systems that protect water quality. The study provides cities and regulators with scientific evidence that existing biofilters can effectively reduce the amount of microplastic pollution that reaches California's coast, while offering clear recommendations for optimizing future designs.

This project is funded by the California Ocean Protection Council (OPC) under Agreement No.C0223003, and is administered by California Sea Grant.
